candidates.application_scope: Syntax and semantics for position-based and regularly spaced iteration.

candidates.name: Iterate numerical drivers and inline macro expansion
candidates.reason: Iterate combines explicit numeric drivers with ordinary element drivers, offering a model for index pairing and regular strides while expanding the iteration into inline code.
candidates.application_scope: Readable, extensible iteration notation and a compiler-visible representation of numeric stepping.
candidates.constraints_or_caveat: Its macro system and code walking do not transfer directly to Python; downward iteration uses a positive stride magnitude, and changing runtime bindings cannot silently inherit macro expansion semantics.
candidates.date_evidence: The opened manual explicitly records a 2006 adaptation of a 1989 original memo; the consulted numerical chapter belongs to that later adaptation, so its exact wording is not backdated.

candidates.name: Cython typed integer-loop lowering
candidates.reason: Cython provides a concrete reference for lowering recognizable numeric range loops into simple machine-level loops when the induction type and stride direction are known.
candidates.application_scope: Optimization conditions, bounds-and-stride notation, and semantic checks before loop lowering.
candidates.constraints_or_caveat: This is a later compiler with explicit C types; overflow timing can change, its relational for-from syntax is deprecated, and the inspected documentation does not prove that arbitrary redefinition of Python builtins is preserved.
candidates.date_evidence: The opened Language Basics page identifies version 3.4.0a0 and a 2026 copyright; the linked differences page identifies version 3.3.0. These are later documentation editions, not evidence of availability in 2000.

candidates.reason: Its iterator-backed range and index-element adapter show how numeric progression and position-aware iteration can be separate, composable operations with explicit start, stop, and step.
candidates.application_scope: Compact range representation, stride iteration, and exposing element positions.
candidates.constraints_or_caveat: This C++17 library is later evidence, its zero-step range is empty rather than an error, and its binding and lifetime rules cannot be copied into dynamic Python unchanged.
candidates.date_evidence: The opened source license states copyright 2013, while the current README explicitly targets C++17; no pre-2000 availability is claimed.

candidates.name: more-itertools numeric_range and islice_extended
candidates.reason: The library separates arithmetic progression from start/stop/step selection of an existing iterable, helping avoid manually combining length and stride calculations for different iteration tasks.
candidates.application_scope: Library-level range objects and selecting regularly spaced elements.
candidates.constraints_or_caveat: Ordinary callable names remain rebindable; negative slicing may need buffering, generic numeric arithmetic can have precision concerns, and these APIs do not by themselves settle mutation-during-iteration semantics.
candidates.date_evidence: The consulted documentation is version 11.2.1; its history places numeric_range in 3.1.0 and includes explicit 2019 and post-2025 release context, with a 2012 copyright footer. An exact introduction date was not established.

raw_response:
# C09 — catalogue-based design references

I found five candidates through opened awesome lists, then followed links to verify them. They are possible design inputs, not claims of deployment or demonstrated benefit. The decision cutoff is 2000-11-01: the current Lisp references describe older designs, but I have not treated their live text as a verified pre-cutoff edition.

1. **Common Lisp LOOP arithmetic clauses** — https://www.lispworks.com/documentation/HyperSpec/Body/m_loop.htm
   Its explicit start, boundary, direction, and stride clauses provide a readable model for generating loop indices without first constructing a numeric sequence. This is useful when positions or every second position are needed. The transfer cost is a substantial iteration sublanguage, and Python would still need precise endpoint, evaluation, mutation, and binding rules. Discovery: https://github.com/vindarel/curated-awesome-cl, followed through its linked iteration guide. Date status: **unknown** for the consulted live edition. The publisher identifies a 1994 source standard, but the live HyperSpec copyright spans 1996-2005.

2. **Iterate numerical drivers and inline macro expansion** — https://iterate.common-lisp.dev/doc/Numerical-Iteration.html
   Iterate combines numeric and element drivers, making an element-plus-position loop or regularly spaced traversal explicit, while its macro implementation generates inline iteration code. Its numerical clauses distinguish inclusive from exclusive endpoints; downward iteration uses a positive stride magnitude. A Python adaptation cannot assume Lisp's macro and code-walking machinery or silently replace runtime binding semantics. Discovery: https://github.com/vindarel/curated-awesome-cl, then the linked iteration guide and official manual. Date status: **post-decision evidence**: the consulted manual states that it is a 2006 adaptation of a 1989 original; I did not verify this exact numerical chapter in the original.

3. **Cython typed integer-loop lowering** — https://cython.readthedocs.io/en/latest/src/userguide/language_basics.html
   This is a concrete implementation reference for optimizing a numeric loop when the induction variable's type and stride direction are known. The documentation also presents a relational bounds-and-stride form, now deprecated, and records that conversion can change when overflow is reported. It does not establish a safe optimization rule for every redefinition of Python's builtin names. Discovery: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vinta/awesome-python/master/README.md. Date status: **post-decision evidence**, from current Cython 3.x documentation with a 2026 copyright on the inspected language chapter.

4. **CPPItertools range and enumerate** — https://github.com/ryanhaining/cppitertools
   Iterator-backed numeric ranges and an index-element adapter offer a model for keeping number generation separate from position-aware traversal. The range has start, stop, and step, supports descent, and can be indexed. Important transfer limits are its C++ binding/lifetime model and its choice to make zero stride produce an empty range. Discovery: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp/master/README.md. Date status: **post-decision evidence**; the opened license is dated 2013 and the current interface targets C++17.

5. **more-itertools numeric_range and islice_extended** — https://more-itertools.readthedocs.io/en/stable/api.html
   These APIs separate generating a numeric progression from selecting start/stop/step positions in an existing iterable, reducing the need for manual length-and-stride arithmetic. The documented numeric progression supports descending steps and rejects zero. Callable rebinding remains possible, and buffering, numeric precision, and mutation behavior require attention. Discovery: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vinta/awesome-python/master/README.md. Date status: **post-decision evidence**, from version 11.2.1 documentation; the exact introduction date was not pinned.

## Translation to the design problem

The useful distinction is between generating numbers, selecting elements at a stride, and pairing each element with its position. Making these operations explicit can improve readability because the programmer no longer has to encode every task as length arithmetic followed by indexing.

Compiler optimization is a separate obligation. As a design inference, a compiler must not lower a call merely because its spelling resembles a familiar builtin: that name may resolve to user code. A fixed language construct could expose dedicated stepping semantics; a callable API would need a proven binding, a runtime identity guard with fallback, or ordinary dynamic execution. None of the inspected libraries alone settles that choice for Python.

For mutation, a numeric progression can keep its own bounds stable, but deleting or inserting source elements can still invalidate or shift positions. A transferred design should specify whether bounds are captured once, how descending and empty ranges work, what zero stride does, and how numeric overflow or non-integer steps behave. These are proposed review questions, not claims about the target proposal.
